title_en: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Changzhou New District Branch v. Kangmei Company — dispute over a loan contract
ruling_gist_en: According to Article 75(4) of the Security Law of the PRC, a loan made by means of export tax rebate account custody constitutes a pledge of the right to export tax rebate. full_text_en:
New District Sub-branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China in Changzhou v. Kangmei Garment Co., Ltd. — dispute over loan contract

【Ruling Summary】

According to Article 75(4) of the Security Law, a loan based on the托管 of an export tax rebate account constitutes a pledge of the right to export tax rebates. When the lender is unable to obtain repayment of the loan, it has the right to be repaid in priority from the borrower's export tax rebates.

Plaintiff: New District Sub-branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China in Changzhou, domiciled at: Changjiang Road, Changzhou City, Jiangsu Province. Person in charge: Wang Chao, branch manager.

Defendant: Changzhou Kangmei Garment Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Sanjing Township, Changzhou City, Jiangsu Province. Legal representative: Meng Guojin, chairman of the board.

Defendant: Changzhou Kangsheng Garment Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Sanjing Township, Changzhou City, Jiangsu Province. Legal representative: Meng Guojin, chairman of the board.

The plaintiff, New District Sub-branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China in Changzhou (hereinafter referred to as "New District Sub-branch"), filed a lawsuit with the Intermediate People's Court of Changzhou City, Jiangsu Province, against the defendants Changzhou Kangmei Garment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Kangmei Company") and Changzhou Kangsheng Garment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Kangsheng Company") over a dispute concerning a loan contract.

The plaintiff, New District Sub-branch, alleged: The defendant Kangmei Company, using its export tax rebate rights as a pledge, borrowed a total of RMB 7.5 million from the plaintiff on two separate occasions. The defendant Kangsheng Company voluntarily assumed joint and several guarantor liability for Kangmei Company's loan with its real property. After the loan was made, Kangmei Company repaid part of the loan. Currently, it still owes a principal of RMB 6,328,382.72 and corresponding interest. However, the company has already encountered circumstances under which the lender is entitled to accelerate repayment of the entire loan as stipulated in the loan contract. The plaintiff requested a judgment ordering Kangmei Company to repay the outstanding principal and corresponding interest, confirming that the plaintiff has the right to be repaid in priority from Kangmei Company's export tax rebates, and ordering Kangsheng Company to assume joint and several liability for Kangmei Company's debts.

The defendant Kangmei Company argued: Although the facts regarding the loan amount and the pledge of export tax rebates as alleged by the plaintiff are true, the defendant has fallen into financial difficulties due to involvement in numerous economic disputes. Although it has ceased operations, it is still making every effort to repay the plaintiff, and has not intentionally defaulted. The defendant Kangsheng Company raised no objection to the plaintiff's claims.

The Intermediate People's Court of Changzhou City found the following facts upon trial:

On December 18, 2003, the defendant Kangmei Company issued a "Commitment Letter for Export Tax Rebate Special Account" to the plaintiff New District Sub-branch, undertaking to use its export tax rebate rights as security for a loan from New District Sub-branch. If the company failed to repay the loan as agreed in the loan contract, New District Sub-branch was entitled to deduct the loan principal and interest from the export tax rebate special account (account number 1105021629001001561) opened by the company with New District Sub-branch. In an attached "Confirmation Form for Export Tax Rebate Account Trusteeship Loan Business," the Changzhou Municipal Bureau of State Taxation confirmed that, as of December 18, 2003, Kangmei Company's outstanding and unrefunded tax rebate amounted to RMB 13,513,100. On December 25, 2003, the defendant Kangmei Company and the plaintiff New District Sub-branch entered into a loan contract stipulating that Kangmei Company would borrow RMB 4.5 million from New District Sub-branch, with a loan term from December 25, 2003 to June 22, 2004, and a monthly interest rate of 5.04‰. At the same time, Kangmei Company and New District Sub-branch also entered into a pledge contract of rights, stipulating that Kangmei Company would pledge its export tax rebate rights to New District Sub-branch as security for the loan. After the contract was signed, New District Sub-branch disbursed RMB 4.5 million to Kangmei Company as agreed. On February 20, 2004, the defendant Kangmei Company and the plaintiff New District Sub-branch entered into another loan contract stipulating that Kangmei Company would borrow RMB 3 million from New District Sub-branch, with a loan term from February 20, 2004 to August 8, 2004, and a monthly interest rate of 5.04‰. At the same time, the parties also entered into a pledge contract of rights, stipulating that Kangmei Company would pledge its export tax rebate rights to New District Sub-branch as security for the loan. After the contract was signed, New District Sub-branch disbursed RMB 3 million to Kangmei Company as agreed.

On April 22, 2004, the defendant Kangmei Company repaid the plaintiff New District Sub-branch RMB 500,000 of the loan principal. On June 7, the defendant Kangsheng Company issued a commitment letter to New District Sub-branch, stating that it voluntarily assumed joint and several guarantor liability for Kangmei Company's loan with its real property. On June 14, New District Sub-branch sent a notice to Kangmei Company to accelerate repayment of the entire loan on the ground that the circumstances stipulated in the contract had occurred, and Kangmei Company raised no objection. On June 24, New District Sub-branch filed the lawsuit. On July 29, Kangmei Company repaid another RMB 671,617.28 of the loan principal to New District Sub-branch. Both parties confirmed the above facts, and they are hereby affirmed.

The issue in dispute in this case is: Whether a loan based on the trusteeship of an export tax rebate account can be recognized as a pledge loan? Whether the plaintiff has a pledge right over the defendant's export tax rebates?

One view holds that there is no legal basis for recognizing a loan based on the trusteeship of an export tax rebate account as a pledge loan, and therefore the plaintiff cannot be deemed to have a pledge right over the defendant's export tax rebates. The reasons are:

1. The export tax rebate funds in an export tax rebate account are tax refunds that the tax authority, subject to certain conditions, returns to the export enterprise as a taxpayer. Before the tax authority has reviewed and approved the refund and actually refunded it to the export enterprise, the export enterprise does not possess these funds but only enjoys the right to claim the refund from the tax authority. Therefore, the export tax rebate funds in the account are not property in the civil law sense, but merely a right of the account holder. Since this right is exercised against the tax authority, an administrative agency, the legal relationship between the right holder and the obligor is unequal and belongs to the realm of public law. Therefore, this right is not transferable. The subject matter of a pledge right must possess the characteristics of property and transferability; export tax rebates clearly do not meet these two conditions. The so-called pledge of the right to export tax rebates involves a right under administrative law, not a civil right between equal parties. Since such a right cannot be transferred, it cannot be pledged.

2. Article 85 of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Security Law of the People's Republic of China" provides: "If a debtor or a third party specificizes money in the form of a special account, sealed money, margin money, etc., and delivers it to the creditor for possession as security for a debt, and the debtor fails to perform the debt, the creditor may be repaid in priority from such money." As stated above, the export tax rebate funds in an export tax rebate account are merely a right of the account holder, not actual money; before the tax authority has reviewed and approved the refund and actually refunded it, it is only an expected property that may or may not be realized for the account holder, and it cannot be "specificized" at all. Therefore, a loan in the form of trusteeship of an export tax rebate account is not a pledge of money referred to in this judicial interpretation.

3. The current export tax rebate account trusteeship loan business conducted by the banking industry originated from the "Notice on Handling Export Tax Rebate Account Trusteeship Loan Business" issued by superior banks. Article 4 of this notice provides: "Export tax rebate account trusteeship loans are commercial loans, independently reviewed and decided by commercial banks. Commercial banks shall agree with the borrower that, from the date the bank disburses the loan until the loan is fully repaid, the borrower agrees that the lender may monitor the account, and without the lender's consent, the borrower may not unilaterally transfer funds out of the account. The tax rebate funds in the export tax rebate special account are the guarantee for the export enterprise to repay the loan. Commercial banks shall require the enterprise to repay the principal and interest of the loan after the tax rebate funds are received. If necessary, commercial banks may require the export enterprise to provide other guarantees based on the risk level of the loan." This is the most complete expression of the purpose of export tax rebate account trusteeship loans. This departmental regulation only mentions that banks may trusteeship export tax rebate accounts; it does not provide for a pledge, and throughout the text, the word "pledge" is not used, nor is any priority right of the bank mentioned. Therefore, it cannot serve as a basis for a bank to exercise a pledge right. Recognizing a loan based on the trusteeship of an export tax rebate account as a pledge loan lacks legal basis.

Another view holds that a loan based on the trusteeship of an export tax rebate account should be recognized as a pledge loan, and the plaintiff has a pledge right over the defendant's export tax rebates. The reasons are:

1. The Security Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Security Law") provides for two types of pledges: personal property pledges and rights pledges. The rights that serve as the subject matter of a rights pledge must have the characteristics of property and transferability. Property means that the right can be manifested as material wealth owned by a person; transferability means that the right must be exchangeable and have exchange value. Although the right to export tax rebates is an anticipated interest, this interest is realized in the form of a certain amount of export tax rebate funds, which constitute material wealth owned by a person; export tax rebates are directly expressed in monetary amounts. When the tax rebate funds are deposited into the export tax rebate special account, the right to export tax rebates is realized as export tax rebate funds. The realization function of the right to export tax rebates gives it transferability. Since export tax rebates are a right enjoyed by export enterprises and possess property and transferability, they can certainly serve as the subject matter of a rights pledge.

2. In accordance with the spirit of the Security Law, the pledgor and the pledgee shall enter into a pledge contract in writing, and the pledge contract becomes effective when the pledged property is delivered to and possessed by the pledgee; for a rights pledge, the parties shall register with the competent authority for the administration of such rights. In this case, the parties entered into a written pledge contract, clearly stating that the defendant Kangmei Company pledged its export tax rebate rights to the plaintiff New District Sub-branch. Pursuant to the pledge contract, Kangmei Company opened an export tax rebate special account with New District Sub-branch and authorized New District Sub-branch to deduct the loan principal and interest from the tax rebate special account. This pledge relationship between the parties has been registered for the record with the tax authority, and Kangmei Company's tax rebate account number and tax rebate amount have been confirmed by the tax authority; until the loan is fully repaid, without the consent of New District Sub-branch, the tax authority will not handle the transfer of Kangmei Company's account. Through this monitoring of the export tax rebate account, New District Sub-branch ensures that Kangmei Company's tax rebate funds can only be deposited into this single account. This "trusteeship" of the account enables New District Sub-branch to possess and control Kangmei Company's right to export tax rebates. Such possession and control of a right is the essence of a rights pledge; and registration for the record with the tax authority serves as the public notification of the pledge of the right to export tax rebates, thereby creating legal effect against third parties.

3. Although there is currently no explicit provision in Chinese law regarding the use of the right to export tax rebates as a pledge, such use has objectively existed in practice. This fact demonstrates that this form of security is beneficial for helping enterprises alleviate the financial strain caused by delays in export tax rebates, solving the loan guarantee problem for some foreign trade export enterprises, and expanding financing channels. Recognizing this new type of security that has developed in practice as valid is of great significance for facilitating capital circulation and commodity circulation, ensuring transaction security and the realization of creditor's rights, and stabilizing the social and economic order. If this type of security were denied, its security function would undoubtedly be weakened, making it incapable of having effect against third parties or binding the borrower, and the creditor's claim would be difficult to protect.

The Intermediate People's Court of Changzhou City held:

Article 207 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If a borrower fails to repay the loan within the agreed term, it shall pay overdue interest in accordance with the agreement or relevant state provisions." Article 6 of the Security Law provides: "For the purposes of this Law, 'guaranty' means that a surety and a creditor agree that, when the debtor fails to perform its debts, the surety shall perform the debts or assume liability in accordance with the agreement." Article 75(4) provides that other rights that may be pledged according to law may be pledged.

The loan contract entered into between the defendant Kangmei Company and the plaintiff New District Sub-branch is lawful and valid. During the performance of the loan contract, because circumstances occurred under which the lender was entitled to accelerate repayment of the entire loan as stipulated in the contract, New District Sub-branch demanded accelerated repayment of the entire loan, and Kangmei Company raised no objection. Kangmei Company currently owes New District Sub-branch a loan principal of RMB 6,328,382.72, which it shall repay along with corresponding interest and overdue interest.

At the same time as the loan contract was signed, the defendant Kangmei Company and the plaintiff New District Sub-branch also entered into a pledge contract for the right to export tax rebates, stipulating that Kangmei Company would pledge its export tax rebate rights to New District Sub-branch as security for Kangmei Company's loan from New District Sub-branch. Pursuant to the pledge contract, Kangmei Company opened an export tax rebate special account with New District Sub-branch, and this account along with Kangmei Company's outstanding and unrefunded tax rebate amount of RMB 13.51 million were confirmed by the Changzhou Municipal Bureau of State Taxation. Therefore, the export tax rebate account trusteeship loan between Kangmei Company and New District Sub-branch constitutes a pledge of the right to export tax rebates, and New District Sub-branch has the right to be repaid in priority from Kangmei Company's export tax rebates. The defendant Kangsheng Company issued a commitment letter to New District Sub-branch, voluntarily assuming joint and several guarantor liability for Kangmei Company's loan. This commitment does not violate legal provisions. The claims of New District Sub-branch should be upheld.

Accordingly, on September 2, 2004, the Intermediate People's Court of Changzhou City rendered the following judgment:

1. The defendant Kangmei Company shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, repay the plaintiff New District Sub-branch the loan principal of RMB 6,328,382.72, and pay the interest accrued up to the date of this judgment in the amount of RMB 133,267.93.

2. To the extent that the above debts are not satisfied, the plaintiff New District Sub-branch has the right to be repaid in priority from the defendant Kangmei Company's export tax rebates.

3. The defendant Kangsheng Company shall assume joint and several liability for the above debts of the defendant Kangmei Company.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 45,193 and property preservation fee of RMB 35,520 shall be borne by the defendant Kangmei Company.

After the judgment was announced, neither party appealed.
